'''Jeffrey Robert Forshaw''' [[Fellow of the Royal Society|FRS]] (born 1968)<ref>{{cite web|title=Professor Jeffrey Robert Forshaw of Atherton|url=http://www.atherton.towntalk.co.uk/local/famous-people/d/649/professor-jeffrey-robert-forshaw/|website=TownTalk|access-date=14 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220172741/http://www.atherton.towntalk.co.uk/local/famous-people/d/649/professor-jeffrey-robert-forshaw/|archive-date=20 December 2016}}</ref> is a British [[theoretical physicist]] and [[particle physicist]] with a special interest in [[quantum chromodynamics|quantum chromodynamics (QCD)]]: the study of the behaviour of subatomic particles, using data from the [[HERA (particle accelerator)|HERA particle accelerator]], [[Tevatron]] [[particle accelerator]]<ref name="CoxForshaw1999">{{cite journal|last1=Cox|first1=Brian|last2=Forshaw|first2=Jeff|last3=Lönnblad|first3=Leif|title=Hard colour singlet exchange at the Tevatron|journal=[[Journal of High Energy Physics]]|volume=1999|issue=10|year=1999|page=023|doi=10.1088/1126-6708/1999/10/023|arxiv=hep-ph/9908464|bibcode=1999JHEP...10..023C|s2cid=2081010}}</ref> and the [[Large Hadron Collider|Large Hadron Collider (LHC)]] at [[CERN]].<ref name=ButterworthCox2002>{{cite journal|last1=Butterworth|first1=J. M.|author-link1=Jon Butterworth|last2=Cox|first2=B. E.|last3=Forshaw|first3=J. R.|title=WW scattering at the CERN LHC|journal=Physical Review D|volume=65|issue=9|year=2002|article-number=096014|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.65.096014|arxiv=hep-ph/0201098|bibcode=2002PhRvD..65i6014B|s2cid=118887006|url=http://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/9349/1/9349.pdf}}</ref> He is Professor of Theoretical Physics in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the [[University of Manchester]].<ref name="rs2026">{{cite web |title=Exceptional scientists elected as Fellows of the Royal Society |url=https://royalsociety.org/news/2026/05/new-fellows-announcement-2026/ |website=Royal Society |date=27 May 2026 |access-date=28 May 2026}}</ref>

He is the co-author of five books, including the [[popular science]] books ''[[Why Does E=mc²?]]'', ''[[The Quantum Universe]]'' and ''Universal: A guide to the cosmos'', co-written with physicist [[Brian Cox (physicist)|Brian Cox]]. He has also written over 100 [[peer review]]ed papers published in [[scientific journal]]s<ref name=orcid/><ref name=scopus>{{Scopus|id=7003356195}}</ref><ref name="hep2016">{{cite web|title=Jeff Forshaw publications|url=http://inspirehep.net/search?p=f+a+forshaw|website=[[INSPIRE-HEP]]|access-date=30 November 2016}}</ref><ref name="uom22016">{{cite web|title=List of publications|url=http://www.manchester.ac.uk/research/jeffrey.forshaw/publications|website=University of Manchester|access-date=7 December 2016}}</ref> and speaks at international science festivals for children and adults. He frequently acts as science consultant to the BBC and other media<ref name=srm2016/> and is a [[columnist]] for ''[[The Observer]]''.

Forshaw is a recipient of the [[Maxwell Medal and Prize]] for his contribution to particle physics, and the [[Kelvin Prize]] from the [[Institute of Physics]] for his contribution to the public understanding of physics.<ref>[http://www.physics.manchester.ac.uk/people/staff-spotlights/jeff-forshaw/ Professor Jeff Forshaw at University of Manchester School of Physics and Astronomy]</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Jeff Forshaw |website=[[The Guardian]] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230329165446/https://www.theguardian.com/profile/jeff-forshaw |archive-date=29 March 2023 |url-status=live |url=https://www.theguardian.com/profile/jeff-forshaw}}</ref><ref>[http://eu.wiley.com/WileyCDA/Section/id-817222.html TED Studies: Physics – The Edge of Knowledge]</ref>

==Education==
Forshaw attended Hesketh Fletcher High School<ref>{{cite web|title=Ex-Wigan Tech student excited by 'God Particle' discovery|url=http://www.wigantoday.net/news/ex-wigan-tech-student-excited-by-god-particle-discovery-1-4711947|website=Wigan Today|publisher=Johnston Publishing|access-date=7 December 2016}}</ref> and studied [[A levels]] at [[Wigan and Leigh College]] where he considered his teachers, Jim Breithaupt, Alan Skinner and Jean Wadsworth an important influence on his future career.<ref name="wal2016">{{cite web|author=Anon|year=2014|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161214231328/https://www.wigan-leigh.ac.uk/blog/post/jeff-forshaw-aoc-roll-of-honour|archive-date=14 December 2016|title=Professor Makes Roll of Honour|url=https://www.wigan-leigh.ac.uk/blog/post/jeff-forshaw-aoc-roll-of-honour|website=Wigan & Leigh College|access-date=30 November 2016}}</ref> He went on to study physics at [[Oriel College, Oxford]]<ref name=orcid>Jeff Forshaw {{ORCID|0000-0001-9590-7390}}</ref> graduating with a first class [[Bachelor of Arts]] degree in physics in 1989,<ref name="srm2016">{{cite web|title=Professor Jeff Forshaw|url=http://www.sueridermanagement.co.uk/presenters/ProfJeffForshaw/JeffForshaw.htm|website=Sue Rider Management|access-date=30 November 2016|archive-date=6 February 2009|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090206073110/http://www.sueridermanagement.co.uk/presenters/ProfJeffForshaw/JeffForshaw.htm}}</ref> followed by a [[PhD]] in [[Theoretical Physics]] from the University of Manchester in 1992 for research on the [[Parton (particle physics)|parton content]] of the [[photon]] and photon-induced minijets.<ref>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Manchester|title=The Parton content of the photon and photon-induced minijets|first=Jeffrey Robert|last=Forshaw|date=1992|url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.679960|access-date=14 December 2016|archive-date=8 November 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221108095552/https://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.679960}}</ref><ref name="ocr2016">{{cite web|title=KS4 Speaker Biographies|url=http://www.ocr.org.uk/Images/15538-view-speakers-biographies.pdf|website=OCR|access-date=7 December 2016}}</ref>

==Career and research==
From 1992 to 1995, he worked as a [[postdoctoral research]] scientist at the [[Rutherford Appleton Laboratory]]<ref name=orcid/> near [[Didcot]] in Oxfordshire, in the group led by noted particle physicist [[Frank Close]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Brian Cox & Jeff Forshaw|url=http://www.dianebanks.co.uk/science-current-affairs-and-history-authors/brian-cox-jeff-forshaw|website=Diane Banks|access-date=13 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161221015725/http://www.dianebanks.co.uk/science-current-affairs-and-history-authors/brian-cox-jeff-forshaw|archive-date=21 December 2016}}</ref>  While studying he intended to become a school teacher but began lecturing at university level after his PhD.<ref name="ns2016">{{cite web|last1=Lewis|first1=Helen|author-link=Helen Lewis (journalist)|title=Science tells you that your opinion is worthless. That's difficult|url=http://www.newstatesman.com/scitech/2011/12/interview-science-cox-physics|website=New Statesman|date=8 December 2011 |access-date=7 December 2016}}</ref> He began his friendship and eventual collaboration with [[Brian Cox (physicist)|Brian Cox]] around 1995 when he was Cox's lecturer in Advanced [[Quantum Field Theory]] as they were the same age, despite being student and teacher.<ref name="hwm2016">{{cite web|last1=Duerden|first1=Nick|last2=Jacques|first2=Adam|title=How We Met|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/news/people/profiles/how-we-met-professor-brian-cox-professor-jeff-forshaw-we-argue-all-the-time-9386798.html|website=The Independent|date=16 May 2014 |access-date=7 December 2016}}</ref>

In 2004, he became professor of [[particle physics]] at the [[University of Manchester School of Physics and Astronomy]].<ref name="uom2016">{{cite web|last1=Forshaw|first1=Jeff|title=School of Physics and Astronomy|url=http://www.physics.manchester.ac.uk/people/staff-spotlights/jeff-forshaw/|website=University of Manchester|access-date=30 November 2016}}</ref><ref name=srm2016/> At Manchester he engaged in experimental and theoretical research in the field of particle physics, with particular interest in the behaviours of particles in high energy colliders as at the [[ATLAS experiment]] and [[Compact Muon Solenoid|Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS)]] experiments, part of the [[Large Hadron Collider]] particle accelerator research at [[CERN]] in [[Geneva]], Switzerland.<ref name=uom2016/> He said of his theoretical physics research, {{Cquote|text=As a theoretical physicist, most of my time is spent doing calculations that are wrong. It's a humbling exercise, a massive dose of humility.<ref name=ns2016/>}}

He has written over 100 peer-reviewed articles in scientific journals, including papers on ordering [[gluon]] emissions, [[quantum field theory]] and [[Holographic principle|holographic]] wavefunction of [[mesons]].<ref name=hep2016/> Forshaw and his frequent co-author Cox have stated the [[peer review]] process of science results publishing is important because it ensures that minimum standards are met in the scientific community and gives due attribution to all associates working on the piece who are finalising the presentation of the paper, and [[blogging]] research before it is published should be avoided.<ref name=gua22016/>

[[File:1 - Jeff Forshaw, QED Con 2017.jpg|thumb|right|Forshaw at [[QED (conference)|QED: Question, Explore, Discover]] conference, 2017]]
As an educator, Forshaw is keen to encourage the idea that basic principles and theories in particle physics should be introduced to children in school in order to encourage understanding of the [[scientific method]] and use of [[Evidence-based education|evidence-based thinking]] at a young age.<ref name="yt2016">{{cite web|title=Informal interview with Brian Cox and Jeff Forshaw at the British Science Festival 2012|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BupoASal1e8|website=YouTube| date=23 September 2012 |access-date=7 December 2016}}</ref><ref name="ft2016">{{cite web|last1=Cook|first1=Chris|title=In pursuit of the universe: Brian Cox and Jeff Forshaw|url=https://www.ft.com/content/a6a7c4d6-0024-11e1-8441-00144feabdc0|website=Financial Times|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref>

In 2008, he added his voice to the [[Science and Technology Facilities Council|Science and Technology Facilities Council (STFC)]] campaign against spending cuts to UK physics budgets in a letter to the then Secretary of State at the [[Department for Innovation, Universities and Skills]], [[John Denham (politician)|John Denham]], which was signed by around 350 prominent physicists from the UK theoretical particle physics community.<ref name=cuts2016>{{cite web|title=Letter to the Secretary of State|url=http://www.hep.ucl.ac.uk/~markl/pp/theory_letter.pdf|website=University College London|access-date=12 December 2016|archive-date=15 October 2008|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081015160219/http://www.hep.ucl.ac.uk/~markl/pp/theory_letter.pdf}}</ref> The letter pointed out the adverse effects the cuts would have, not only to physics research in the UK, but also in discouraging future students of astronomy, particle physics and science in general.<ref name=cuts2016/> When asked whether investment in physics could potentially contribute to the UK economy he pointed out, {{Cquote|text=The world has been revolutionised by fundamental research into quantum physics done 60 years ago and now there are billions of transistors inside every home computer. They are a key ingredient of the microchip.<ref name="guard2016">{{cite web|title=Brian Cox and Jeff Forshaw explain the big bang|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2011/oct/23/brian-cox-jeff-forshaw-answers|website=The Guardian|date=22 October 2011 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref>}} He also encourages people to see the relevance of [[quantum physics]] in everyday life and not purely as an academic discipline, using solar panels and lasers as examples of practical everyday applications.<ref name=ns2016/> In his many public lectures he has been described as "deeply enthusiastic about his subject"<ref name="Ymix2016">{{cite web|last1=Cawte|first1=Heather|title=Review: The Quantum Universe – talk by Professor Jeff Forshaw|url=http://www.yorkmix.com/things-to-do/reviews/review-the-quantum-universe-talk-by-professor-jeff-forshaw/|website=York Mix|access-date=13 December 2016|archive-date=16 April 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160416152630/http://www.yorkmix.com/things-to-do/reviews/review-the-quantum-universe-talk-by-professor-jeff-forshaw/}}</ref> and "entertaining and informative."<ref>{{cite web|title=Jeff Forshaw's talk – a write-up|url=https://bollingtonscibar.wordpress.com/2011/09/23/jeff-forshaws-talk-a-write-up/|website=Bollington SciBar|date=23 September 2011 |access-date=13 December 2016}}</ref>
Forshaw often visits schools and colleges to speak in front of young people about aspects of his work<ref name="star2016">{{cite web|title=Star Lecture archive – Jeff Forshaw|url=http://www.manchester.ac.uk/discover/events/star-lectures/archive-forshaw/|website=University of Manchester|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref><ref name="stp2016">{{cite web|title=The Quantum Universe|url=https://www.stpetersyork.org.uk/st_peters/news_calendar/public_lectures/the_quantum_universe|website=St. Peter's York|access-date=12 December 2016|archive-date=20 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220132618/https://www.stpetersyork.org.uk/st_peters/news_calendar/public_lectures/the_quantum_universe}}</ref> and has appeared on children's television in the UK explaining concepts such as the [[Higgs boson]] on [[BBC television]] programme [[Newsround]] for children aged six to twelve.<ref>{{cite news|last1=Newsround|title=Brian Cox's on the spot|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/av/18634684|website=BBC|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Newsround|title=Historic Higgs boson discovery – it "could" exist|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/18701498|website=BBC|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|last1=Newsround|title=Professor Jeff Forshaw explains Higgs boson|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/newsround/av/18701499|website=BBC|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> He is an ambassador for educational charity [[Potential Plus UK]] which aims to support the emotional and learning needs of gifted and exceptional children.<ref>{{cite web|title=Become a Potential Plus UK Ambassador|url=http://www.potentialplusuk.org/general_main.php?contentid=487&webid=463#|website=Potential Plus UK|access-date=7 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220105054/http://www.potentialplusuk.org/general_main.php?contentid=487&webid=463|archive-date=20 December 2016}}</ref> Forshaw also regularly contributes at SciBar events (literally science in a bar)<ref name="scibar2016">{{cite web|last1=Wilson|first1=Lorelly|title=North West SciBar Network|url=http://www.britishscienceassociation.org/north-west-scibar-network|website=British Science Association|date=22 June 2015 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> and [[Café Scientifique]] events in the UK.<ref name="uom32016">{{cite web|last1=Haworth|first1=Aeron|title=Physicist honoured for science communication|url=http://www.manchester.ac.uk/discover/news/article/?id=10349|website=University of Manchester|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> He has supervised several PhD students and postdocs.<ref name=delgado>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Manchester|title=Infrared QCD resummations at hadron colliders|first=Rosa Maria|last=Duran Delgado|date=2011|url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.549097|oclc=798401971|access-date=14 December 2016|archive-date=5 August 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200805163322/https://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.549097}} {{open access}}</ref><ref name=reeves>{{cite thesis|degree=PhD|publisher=University of Manchester|title=Aspects of modified gravity|first=Edward|last=Reeves|date=2014|url=http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.603162|oclc=883435893|access-date=14 December 2016|archive-date=20 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220150350/http://ethos.bl.uk/OrderDetails.do?uin=uk.bl.ethos.603162}} {{open access}}</ref><ref name=homepage>{{cite web|url=http://www.hep.man.ac.uk/u/forshaw/ |publisher=University of Manchester |website=hep.man.ac.uk |first=Jeff |last=Forshaw |year=2016 |title=Jeff Forshaw homepage |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161222015507/http://www.hep.man.ac.uk/u/forshaw/ |archive-date=22 December 2016 }}</ref>

===Publications and media===
Forshaw writes frequent [[popular science]] articles explaining complex concepts in physics for the press and magazine publications.<ref>{{cite web|title=Author profile|url=https://www.theguardian.com/profile/jeff-forshaw|website=The Guardian|access-date=7 December 2016}}</ref> He has written on subjects such as [[matter]] and [[antimatter]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Why there is an imbalance between matter and antimatter|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2012/mar/18/matter-antimatter-cern-jeff-forshaw|website=Observer|date=18 March 2012 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> the [[Big Bang]],<ref name=gua22016>{{cite web|title=Brian Cox and Jeff Forshaw explain the big bang|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2011/oct/23/brian-cox-jeff-forshaw-answers|website=Observer|date=22 October 2011 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> the existence of the [[Higgs boson]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Higgs boson to be unveiled (possibly)|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2011/dec/11/higgs-boson-cern-jeff-forshaw|website=Observer|date=11 December 2011 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> [[quantum computers]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Quantum computers are leaping ahead|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2012/may/06/quantum-computing-physics-jeff-forshaw|website=Observer|date=5 May 2012 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> [[supersymmetry]],<ref>{{cite web|title=Supersymmetry: is it really too good not to be true?|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2012/dec/09/supersymmetry-particle-physics-cern-forshaw|website=Observer|date=9 December 2012 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> the [[Planck satellite]],<ref>{{cite web|title=How the dawn of time has a promising future in research|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2013/apr/14/planck-satellite-big-bang-universe-research|website=Observer|date=13 April 2013 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> [[dark matter]]<ref>{{cite web|title=New light cast on dark matter…|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2013/may/26/dark-matter-jeff-forshaw|website=Observer|date=25 May 2013 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> and the technology of [[nuclear fusion]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Nuclear fusion – your time has come|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2012/sep/16/nuclear-fusion-iter-jet-forshaw|website=Observer|date=16 September 2012 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref>
He has also co-authored a set of physics talks with educational support materials for [[TED (conference)|TED]] Studies entitled ''Physics – The Edge of Knowledge'' which is designed to be used online by teachers and students. It explores the relationship between the laws of nature and quantum physics from subatomic particles to the wider universe.<ref name="ted2016">{{cite web|title=TED Studies: Physics – The Edge of Knowledge|url=http://eu.wiley.com/WileyCDA/Section/id-817222.html|website=Wiley|access-date=7 December 2016}}</ref> Other popular science publications include:

*''QCD and the Pomeron'' is a text book written with [[Douglas Ross (physicist)|Douglas A. Ross]] (1997)<ref>{{cite book|last1=Forshaw|first1=Jeffrey R.|last2=Ross|first2=Douglas A.|author-link2=Douglas Ross (physicist)|title=QCD and the Pomeron|date=1997|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=0-521-56880-3}}</ref> written for theoretical and experimental particle physicists and those in the field of [[applied mathematics]] and investigates the [[pomeron]], an object in high energy particle physics. It was described as the "First book on the physics of the pomeron, fills a gaping hole in the literature."<ref>{{cite web|title=Quantum Chromodynamics and the Pomeron|url=http://admin.cambridge.org/sb/academic/subjects/physics/particle-physics-and-nuclear-physics/quantum-chromodynamics-and-pomeron?format=PB&isbn=9780521568807|website=Cambridge University Press|access-date=12 December 2016|archive-date=20 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220202604/http://admin.cambridge.org/sb/academic/subjects/physics/particle-physics-and-nuclear-physics/quantum-chromodynamics-and-pomeron?format=PB&isbn=9780521568807}}</ref>
*''Dynamics and Relativity'' written with Gavin Smith (2009)<ref>{{cite book|last1=Forshaw|first1=Jeff|last2=Smith|first2=Gavin|title=Dynamics and Relativity|date=2009|publisher=Wiley|isbn=978-0-470-01460-8}}</ref> is an undergraduate level text book on the physics behind classical mechanics and relativity.
*''[[Why Does E=mc²?]]'' written with [[Brian Cox (physicist)|Brian Cox]] (2009)<ref name="wde2016">{{cite book|last1=Cox|first1=Brian|author-link=Brian Cox (physicist)|last2=Forshaw|first2=Jeff|title=Why Does E=mc2|date=2009|publisher=Da Capo|isbn=978-0-306-81911-7}}</ref> is a [[popular science]] book exploring [[Theory of relativity|Einstein's Theory of relativity]] and what it means in relation to topics such as the [[Big Bang]] and the [[Large Hadron Collider]]. The book received very positive reviews for being easy to read and entertaining, despite dealing with complex physical theories and mathematics, from newspapers such as ''[[The Guardian]]'',<ref>{{cite web|last1=Jha|first1=Alok|title=Why Does E=mc2? by Brian Cox and Jeff Forshaw – review|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2010/oct/18/einstein-relativity-science-book-review|website=Guardian|date=18 October 2010 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> ''New York Journal of Books''<ref>{{cite web|last1=Storrs|first1=Graham|title=Why Does E=mc2? (And Why Should We Care?)|url=http://www.nyjournalofbooks.com/book-review/why-does-emc2-and-why-should-we-care|website=NYJB|access-date=12 December 2016|archive-date=20 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220163935/http://www.nyjournalofbooks.com/book-review/why-does-emc2-and-why-should-we-care|url-status=dead}}</ref> and ''[[New Scientist]]'',<ref>{{cite web|title=Review: Why Does E = mc2?|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg20227141-700-review-why-does-e-mc2/|website=New Scientist|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> and was shortlisted for the [[Royal Society Prizes for Science Books|Royal Society science book prize]] in 2010.<ref name=matt2016>{{cite web|last1=Matthews|first1=Robert|author-link=Robert Matthews (scientist)|title=Royal Society science book prize|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/news/science/8072485/Royal-Society-science-book-prize-theyre-binding-us-with-science.html|website=Telegraph|date=19 October 2010 |access-date=7 December 2016}}</ref>
*''[[The Quantum Universe]]'' written with Brian Cox (2012)<ref name="qu2016">{{cite book|last1=Cox|first1=Brian|author-link=Brian Cox (physicist)|last2=Forshaw|first2=Jeff|title=The Quantum Universe: Everything that can happen does happen|date=2012|publisher=Penguin|isbn=978-0-241-95270-2}}</ref> is a popular science book that attempts to explain [[quantum physics]]. ''[[Economist]]'' magazine listed it as one of its 'Books of the Year' for 2011.<ref>{{cite journal|title=Books of the Year|url=https://www.economist.com/books-and-arts/2011/12/10/page-turners|journal=The Economist|access-date=13 December 2016}}</ref> It received favourable reviews from ''The Guardian''<ref>{{cite web|last1=Kaiser|first1=David|title=The Quantum Universe by Brian Cox and Jeff Forshaw – review|url=https://www.libreoffice.org/download/libreoffice-fresh/?type=mac-x86_64|website=Guardian|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> and the ''Economist''<ref>{{cite news|title=Big bang|url=https://www.economist.com/books-and-arts/2011/11/05/big-bang|newspaper=The Economist|access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> while ''[[The Daily Telegraph]]'' described it as enjoyable but "not an easy read,"<ref>{{cite web|last1=Kumar|first1=Manjit|title=The Quantum Universe: Everything That Can Happen Does Happen by Brian Cox and Jeff Forshaw: review|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/culture/books/bookreviews/8838837/The-Quantum-Universe-Everything-That-Can-Happen-Does-Happen-byBrian-Cox-and-JeffForshaw-review.html|website=Telegraph|date=23 October 2011 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> and ''[[The Independent]]'' found the theoretical sections stodgy.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Johnstone|first1=Doug|title=The Quantum Universe: Everything That Can Happen Does Happen|url=https://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/books/reviews/the-quantum-universe-everything-that-can-happen-does-happen-by-brian-cox-and-jeff-forshaw-2374486.html#r3z-addoor|website=Independent|date=24 October 2011 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> 
*''Universal, a guide to the cosmos'' written with Brian Cox (2016)<ref name="u2016">{{cite book|last1=Cox|first1=Brian|author-link=Brian Cox (physicist)|last2=Forshaw|first2=Jeff|title=Universal, A Guide to the Cosmos|date=2016|publisher=Penguin|isbn=978-1-84614-436-3}}</ref> explores fundamental questions about the universe and the science of astronomy as it attempts to understand it. ''Universal'' was also well received, with the ''New Scientist'' listing it as one of their ''Great Christmas books'', describing it, "Rarely has a difficult subject been rendered so accessible."<ref>{{cite web|title=Great Christmas books|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/mg23231011-000-great-christmas-books-our-guide-to-gifts-that-keep-on-giving/|website=New Scientist|access-date=13 December 2016}}</ref> ''The Guardian'' referred to it as a [[magnum opus]]<ref>{{cite web|last1=Adams|first1=Tim|title=Brian Cox: 'It's a book about how to think'|url=https://www.theguardian.com/science/2016/sep/18/brian-cox-interview-it-is-a-book-about-how-to-think-universal-a-guide-to-the-cosmos|website=Guardian|date=18 September 2016 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref> and ''[[The Big Issue]]'' focussed on the book's encouragement of critical thinking.<ref name="bi2016">{{cite web|last1=Mackenzie|first1=Steven|title=Professor Brian Cox Interview|url=http://www.bigissue.com/features/interviews/7142/professor-brian-cox-interview-education-is-as-important-to-security-as|website=Big Issue|access-date=12 December 2016|archive-date=28 November 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161128130655/http://www.bigissue.com/features/interviews/7142/professor-brian-cox-interview-education-is-as-important-to-security-as}}</ref> ''Universal'' was featured by [[Fermilab|Symmetry]], the particle physics journal funded by the [[United States Department of Energy|US Department of Energy]] and described as a beautiful book which excels on many levels.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Perricone|first1=Mike|title=Physics books of 2017|url=https://www.symmetrymagazine.org/article/physics-books-of-2017|website=Symmetry|date=12 December 2017 |publisher=Fermilab/SLAC/US Department of Energy|access-date=13 December 2017}}</ref>
*Forshaw is series editor of the ''Manchester Physics Series'' of textbooks aimed at university undergraduates and postgraduates.<ref>{{cite web|title=The Physics of Energy Sources|url=http://eu.wiley.com/WileyCDA/WileyTitle/productCd-1119961688.html|website=John Wiley and sons|access-date=13 December 2016}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=The Manchester Physics Series|url=http://www.physics.manchester.ac.uk/about-us/teaching-and-research/manchester-physics-series/|website=University of Manchester School of Physics and Astronomy|access-date=13 December 2016}}</ref>

Forshaw was science consultant for several [[BBC Television]] series and programmes including the following:

*''[[The Science of Doctor Who]]'', documentary, 2013
*''[[Wonders of Life (TV series)|Wonders of Life]]'' series, 2012
*''[[Wonders of the Universe]]'' series, 2010 and 2011<ref name=uom32016/>
*''A Night With The Stars'', documentary, 2011<ref>{{cite web|title=A Night With the Stars|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt2161319/fullcredits?ref_=tt_ov_st_sm|website=IMDb|access-date=8 May 2017}}</ref>
*''[[Wonders of the Solar System]]'' series, 2009 and 2010
*''[[List of Horizon episodes#Whatonearthsectionlink|Horizon:- What on Earth is wrong with Gravity?]]'' 2009
*''[[List of Horizon episodes#Series 45: 2008–2009|Horizon – Do You Know What Time It Is?]]'' 2008<ref>{{cite web|title=Do You Know What Time It Is|url=https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1332825/fullcredits?ref_=tt_ov_st_sm|website=IMDb|access-date=8 May 2017}}</ref>
*''[[Naked Science]]: Time Machine'' for [[National Geographic (U.S. TV channel)|National Geographic channel]], 2008{{citation needed|date=February 2017}}
*''[[Equinox (TV programme)|Equinox]]: The Big G'', 1998<ref name=srm2016/>

Of his writing and efforts to bring physics to the wider public he said, {{Cquote|text=(Science) is very beautiful...that's why I do it. For me that's the big passion, so that people should get to see how beautiful physics is.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Penguin Books|title=Why does E=mc2 by Brian Cox & Jeff Forshaw|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i-mrj1qrCFk|website=YouTube| date=8 June 2009 |access-date=12 December 2016}}</ref>}}

===Awards and honours===
In 1999, Forshaw was awarded the [[Maxwell Medal and Prize]] from the [[Institute of Physics]] for his outstanding contribution to particle physics.<ref name="iopmax2016">{{cite web|title=Maxwell medal recipients|url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/career/maxwell/medallists/page_38660.html|website=Institute of Physics|access-date=30 November 2016}}</ref> In 2013, Forshaw received the [[Kelvin Medal]] from the [[Institute of Physics]] for his outstanding contribution to making complex physics accessible and understandable to the public.<ref name="iop2016">{{cite web|title=2013 Kelvin medal and prize|url=http://www.iop.org/about/awards/education/kelvin/medallists/page_60409.html|website=Institute of Physics|access-date=30 November 2016}}</ref><ref name=uom32016/> In 2010, Cox and Forshaw's book ''[[Why Does E=mc²?]]'' was shortlisted for the [[Royal Society Prizes for Science Books|Royal Society science book prize]].<ref name=matt2016/> In 2026 he was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]].<ref name="rs2026"/>

==Personal life==
Forshaw lives in Manchester and has two daughters.<ref name=hwm2016/> He was married to scientist and environmental campaigner [[Gail Bradbrook]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.thetimes.com/culture/tv-radio/article/we-re-making-people-s-lives-miserable-but-they-are-talking-about-the-issues-d9hxcp53z|title=Extinction Rebellion founder Gail Bradbrook: 'We're making people's lives miserable but they are talking about the issues'|work=[[The Times]]|date=19 April 2019|last=Billen|first=Andrew|quote=She married another academic, Jeff Forshaw|url-access=subscription}}</ref> He was also married to Naomi Baker, an academic at the University of Manchester, with whom he has two daughters.
